title: First drafts of bid answers from an approved library, reviewed by people
problem: Proposal teams answer hundreds of repeated RFP questions by copy-pasting from old files and chasing subject-matter experts, and half name bandwidth a top challenge.
approach: Approved answers sit in one tagged library; the tool drafts from the best match. Cherry Bekaert uses Loopio; Versent built its own.
A Cherry Bekaert manager says one government audit RFP draft fell from about 8 hours to about 2 (self-reported).
Serco piloted AutogenAI; its case study reports an 85% efficiency gain (vendor-published).
Senior people review and tailor the parts that matter.

title: Search and chat over past proposals and RFPs, with drafting from them
problem: Firms hold hundreds of past proposals, project descriptions and resumes across several systems, so people re-ask marketing for old language and resume versions multiply.
approach: Past proposals go into a searchable store with chat and tagging. Ballard Spahr built 'X-Ray'; Benesch and Woodard & Curran use Kantiv.
A Ballard Spahr partner estimates about 2 hours saved per RFP; Woodard & Curran estimates 30-40% per proposal (self-reported).
Drafts can be checked against the RFP's requirements; no source says who signs off reused content.

title: Pitchbooks, proposals and CVs generated from structured bio and experience data
problem: Pitches are assembled by hand from Word bios and matter lists, experience data sits in spreadsheets, and in one survey only 7% find relevant experience very easy to locate.
approach: An experience platform holds bios, matter experience and CVs as structured data and drafts from templates. GRSM, Stinson and Arup use it.
GRSM's marketing manager says proposal generation time fell by over half in the first quarter (self-reported).
The team tailors each draft, and someone verifies past-matter success stories are accurate.

title: Lawyer bios regenerated from time records, knowledge system and public sites
problem: Baker Botts found itself listed alongside attorneys who had left more than five years earlier, and its generic bios did not surface well in search.
approach: Baker Botts's data science team built a tool using vetted AI that draws on time sheets, its knowledge platform and public websites.
The speaker said bios moved from 'really generic' to more likely to be picked up by AI search (self-reported); no measurement.
The source does not say who signs off a regenerated bio.

title: Reconcile duplicate and stale people and project records before AI proposal retrieval
problem: The same person or project appears under different names across resumes and case studies, so retrieval returns stale records, and one invented citation can disqualify a federal bid.
approach: Before retrieval, the tool extracts roles and dates, matches records for the same person or project, and checks systems of record (vendor-described).
A vendor says an unnamed contractor group caught a disqualifying issue on a bid; no count given (vendor-published).
Staff review and correct merges and splits, verified details are locked, and a person reviews every draft.

title: Pulling requirements and red flags out of RFPs into a compliance matrix
problem: Long RFPs bury mandatory requirements and deadlines, so misses cost disqualification, compliance checks come late and by hand, and teams may spend weeks before spotting an incumbent-friendly bid.
approach: The tool lists every requirement, deadline and mandatory clause in a matrix, then checks the draft against it. Benesch describes this.
In a US government-contracting workshop, an agent also flags vendor-specific requirements and tight timelines, cites pages and drafts clarification questions.
People validate AI output before submission; the bid team investigates each flag and decides whether to pursue.

title: Go/no-go bid decisions informed by experience data and win/loss history
problem: Teams answer more RFPs with less selectivity; decisions run on impressions, and firms cannot quickly tell whether they have done similar work.
approach: Stinson says linking experience data to financial records shows whether it has done similar work before deciding; no figure (vendor-published).
Predictive bid scoring from past pursuits is described only by an ABA column and a vendor blog, so it is an idea.
Leadership decides whether to bid; people sanity-check any AI scoring.

title: Pitch research brief on a client's needs, history and competing firms
problem: Preparing to talk to a client or prospect took hours of gathering documents and data.
approach: Baker Botts's Gemini tool combines public, financial and firm data into client background and a low, medium or high legal-needs score.
Its competitive intelligence director said prep took 24 hours, with a goal to halve it (self-reported). Readout takes about 2 minutes.
The lawyer or business developer reads the readout and decides how to use it.

title: Partners draft urgent pitch responses from firm archives using legal AI
problem: A competitive or urgent request needs experience, prior pitch language and client context pulled from several practice groups and systems, which partners cobble together by hand over days.
approach: Partners query internal archives and filings through a legal AI platform to draft a response.
Harvey says Lynn Pinker Hurst & Schwegmann answered an urgent client request in under 48 hours and won the work (vendor-published).
Lawyers refine and customise the draft for the client.

title: Executive summaries, win themes and one consistent voice across multi-author proposals
problem: Proposals assembled by several partners read as inconsistent, and executive summaries and strategy sections take senior time.
approach: AI drafts executive summaries, rewrites sections to a consistent voice and suggests strategy points for the bid lead to edit.
In Loopio's survey 39% of teams use AI for executive summaries, 28% for brand and voice, 21% for strategy (vendor-published).
Bid teams and partners tailor strategy and nuance in the AI draft.

title: AI check of a proposal's accuracy and compliance before submission
problem: Proposals assert credentials, past performance and staff that buyers may test; AI drafting adds plausible false content, tired reviewers miss gaps, and one invented credential can disqualify.
approach: AI compares draft claims against source records and the solicitation, scores sections against evaluation criteria, and flags unsupported content.
In Loopio's survey 38% of teams use AI to analyse proposal quality and 34% to check accuracy (vendor-published).
A named person signs off each factual claim before submission.

title: Firm-approved AI assistants instead of personal chatbots for proposals and awards
problem: Proposal staff reach for general chatbots the firm does not control, while bid content is confidential; Ballard Spahr leadership saw public ChatGPT privacy and security as a non-starter.
approach: The firm provides approved tools with no-training terms and access controls. Ballard Spahr built 'Ask Ellis' for emails, rewrites and awards submissions.
Ask Ellis has 900 active users across all uses (self-reported).
The firm, not the individual, decides which tools are approved.

title: Tailor each response with AI while keeping the proposal useful as evidence
problem: Tailoring has been a costly signal of quality; once AI makes tailored text cheap, buyers may stop treating it as evidence of fit.
approach: AI drafts text aligned to the RFP; bidders spend the saved effort on editing, evidence and relationship-specific content.
Evidence is adjacent: on a freelance platform, the link between letter alignment and callbacks fell 51% after an AI tool (independent).
The bid lead or partner edits for specific evidence and relationship content.

title: Proposal agents in services platforms that draft from delivery and finance data
problem: Estimates, bids and call notes sit apart from delivery actuals and experience records, so proposals rely on templates or judgment rather than what past work cost and delivered.
approach: Certinia lists an RFP Responder agent, Kantata announced a Sales Accelerator, and Intapp says DealCloud generates pitch documents (vendor-described).
Certinia's headline is proposal creation from 8 hours to 1 (vendor-published), not tied to a customer.
Organisations set approval thresholds before an agent acts, and humans review external communications.

title: People direct AI agents across qualification, drafting and review of bids
problem: AI help is mostly one paragraph at a time, while pursuit work spans qualification, drafting and review, and context built in one person's AI session does not reach the team.
approach: Agents carry out multi-step proposal tasks while people direct and review. Intapp says Celeste can surface pitch material in minutes (vendor claim).
Stinson says it is preparing to adopt agentic capabilities for compliance validation and scoring; no firm runs one end to end.
People direct the agents; no source specifies review gates.

title: Win/loss analytics showing what separates winning proposals from losing ones
problem: Firms judge proposal success only by whether they won; debrief notes and past responses sit apart, so lessons rarely reach the next bid.
approach: Tag each bid with outcome, scores, cost, loss reasons and AI use, then have an assistant read proposals and debriefs together.
Leaders are more likely than novices to use AI on win/loss data, 37% versus 18% (vendor-published); no result published.
People interpret the pattern and decide what changes in the playbook.

title: Idea: answering clients' RFP questions on AI use from a reviewed bank
problem: Idea, not a deployment: many law-firm RFPs now ask which AI tools a firm uses, how they are governed and what savings resulted, while few firms give hard data.
approach: Idea discussed by practitioners: keep a reviewed bank of answers on AI policies, tools and data handling, adapted per RFP.
Back savings claims with a short matter-level evidence pack, and flag conflicts with the client's own AI restrictions.
Partners and risk leaders would approve statements about AI use and savings before bids.

title: Idea: register of AI used in each bid for buyers' disclosure questions
problem: Idea, not a deployment: buyers increasingly ask how AI was used in a bid or will be used in delivery, and the form of the ask varies.
approach: Idea: the bid team records which AI tools touched which sections and what checks were done, and reuses a reviewed disclosure statement.
UK central government offers optional disclosure questions and California requires a clause for generative-AI deliverables; no firm's register was found.
The bid lead reviews the disclosure answer against the register before submission.

title: Idea: flag deal-breaker terms in RFPs and client guidelines before bidding
problem: Idea, not a deployment: client guidelines and RFP terms carry billing, data-security and indemnity provisions that can be deal-breakers; no source measures how late or manually they are reviewed.
approach: Idea from an ABA marketing column: AI compares a client's terms against the firm's standard terms.
It produces a dashboard of clauses that are standard, need review, or are potential deal-breakers. No firm using it was found.
A lawyer reviews flagged clauses and decides whether to bid or negotiate.

title: In-house buyers scope RFPs and compare law-firm proposals with AI (in-house)
problem: In-house legal teams scatter the information needed to choose outside firms, receive long proposals from many firms, and struggle to scope work so bids are comparable.
approach: Priori announced Scout, an agent that recommends a sourcing path, builds the RFP, collects responses and compares proposals; no result published (vendor-published).
An ABA article describes legal operations teams starting to use AI to summarise submissions and flag pricing outliers.
The legal team makes the final firm selection.
